title: Building a hugelkultur bed
subtitle: A wood-core raised bed that improves with age and needs almost no watering.
excerpt: A hugelkultur bed is built over a buried core of logs and woody material. As the wood rots it releases nutrients slowly and holds moisture through dry spells. The mounded shape and increasing organic matter make it more fertile each year.
sourceNotes: Technique documented by Sepp Holzer, Sepp Holzer's Permaculture (2010). UK application notes from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Wood decomposition rates from general forestry and horticulture literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: A raised bed technique in which logs and woody material are buried as a core, then covered with soil, compost, and mulch. The rotting wood acts as a slow-release nutrient and moisture reservoir. The German word means 'hill culture'. The bed typically takes two to three years to reach peak fertility.

content.text: bed converts dead wood into a long-term fertility and moisture reserve. The buried logs decompose slowly over five to ten years. As they rot they hold water during dry spells and release nutrients into the bed above. The mound sinks over time, but soil fertility increases year on year.

Use well-seasoned (but not fully rotten) hardwood logs: oak, ash, alder, apple, hazel, and birch all work well. Avoid fresh conifers, which slow decomposition with their resins, and black walnut, which suppresses plant growth. Small branches and woody prunings can fill gaps between the main logs.

Mark out the bed shape: aim for 1 to 1.5 m wide and as long as needed. Lay logs in a row 20 to 30 cm above ground level. Pack smaller branches and twigs into the gaps. Cover with a layer of compost-rich soil or well-rotted manure, 20 to 30 cm deep. Top with a thick compost mulch and plant into it.

In the first year the wood absorbs some nitrogen as it begins to decompose. Compensate by adding extra compost or a comfrey liquid feed in the first season. From the second year the bed is self-sustaining.

attrs.title: Starting small
attrs.body: A single hugelkultur bed 2 m long and 1 m wide is enough to test the method. Use it for courgettes or squash in the first year (heavy feeders that benefit from the moisture-holding core) and observe how much less it needs watering compared with a flat bed. The results are most obvious in a dry July or August.
